entities.name: Royal Shakespeare Theatre
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Royal Shakespeare Theatre (RST) in Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire, is the primary performance venue of the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC), the world's leading Shakespeare-producing organization, built on the site of earlier Shakespeare theatres destroyed by fire and rebuilt in 1932 as the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre before major renovation completed in 2011. The RST's history — from Victorian memorial to 21st-century thrust stage — mirrors the evolution of Shakespeare performance from reverential monument to living theatre.

The original Shakespeare Memorial Theatre was built in 1879 to commemorate the Tercentenary of Shakespeare's birth. It burned down in 1926 and was replaced by the Elisabeth Scott-designed building (1932), the first major public building in Britain designed by a woman. The 2008-2011 renovation transformed the building from a Victorian proscenium arrangement into a thrust stage with three-sided seating bringing audiences within 15 meters of the actors — a transformation that redefined audience-actor relationship in large-scale Shakespeare performance.

The RSC under Peter Hall's founding directorship (1961) created the most influential Shakespeare producing company in history: Hall, Peter Brook, John Barton, and subsequent directors including Trevor Nunn, Adrian Noble, and Gregory Doran have shaped how Shakespeare is performed globally. The RSC's educational programs, touring productions, and international partnerships make it the world's most significant non-commercial theatre organization. RSC's global reach across 50 countries makes Stratford-upon-Avon the pilgrimage destination for worldwide Shakespeare enthusiasts.
